newsitem.title: CHILE: U.S. eco-millionaire wants national park in Chile.
newsitem.headline: U.S. eco-millionaire wants national park in Chile.

text.p: An American millionaire who bought a wilderness area the size of Rhode Island in southern Chile said on Tuesday he hoped to turn the land into a Chilean national park, despite hostility from local officials.

Douglas Tompkins, multi-millionaire founder of the Esprit clothing chain, said he was surprised at the lack of support in President Eduardo Frei's government for his project to create a vast nature reserve of forests, fjords and mountains.

But he and his supporters among Chilean environmental groups will persevere in efforts to turn the land, covering 1,050 square miles (2,700 sq km) near the city of Puerto Montt, into a nature reserve.

"There are limits to everything. But we would go to extreme lengths before we give up on this project. We will stick with it and persevere," Tompkins told foreign reporters. "And eventually we would even like to see this transferred to the Chilean park authorities as a national park."
Until now, Tompkins has said he wants to turn the land over to a private Chilean foundation on the condition it be opened to the public for tourism.

Tompkins' project has met strong opposition from much of Frei's government, the military and businessmen who think he is bankrolling Chile's environmental movement, which they see as an obstacle for the country's economic development.
But the soft-spoken Californian has strong supporters among politicians and some prominent members of Frei's government.

Tompkins charged this week that he was being harassed. His lawyer said the harassment campaign included death threats, phone taps and air force planes buzzing his home in a remote valley. The government has denied Tompkins' charges.

Parts of the military consider Tompkins a threat to Chile's national security because his land stretches from the Pacific coast to the Argentine border. Air Force commander Fernando Rojas Vender accused Tompkins on Monday of "dismembering" Chile with his purchases.

"I never suspected the government wouldn't support this project. Answering their legitimate concerns, clarifying once and for all that our intentions are not commercial, telling them what we want to do -- I thought they would come around to supporting it," said Tompkins.

Frei's chief political adviser, Juan Villarzu, is expected to release a report this month recommending what official position to take on the project. Tompkins said he was concerned Villarzu had not consulted him in preparation for the report but that he still had confidence in him.

"I understand Villarzu is a level-headed guy and he wants information that is complete and correct," said Tompkins, who lives in a remote valley in southern Chile with his wife, Chris, amid organic garden and virgin forests.
